nodes.label: Current Electricity
nodes.note: Current electricity moves charge through circuits, so resistance, networks, cells, and measurement are the whole syllabus. Its engine is $$V = IR$$ with Kirchhoff's laws supplying the bookkeeping.

nodes.label: Current and Microscopic Transport
nodes.note: Charge in motion is current, and drift velocity explains why a slow electron still delivers steady current. The definitions are $$I = \frac{dQ}{dt}$$ and $$I = neAv_d$$.

nodes.label: Definition of Current
nodes.note: Current is the rate of charge crossing a cross-section, positive by convention: $$I = \frac{dQ}{dt}$$. It is a scalar, and in networks the junction rule keeps it consistent.

nodes.label: Current from a Single Moving Charge
nodes.note: A charge $$q$$ sweeping a length $$d$$ at speed $$v$$ completes a crossing every $$d/v$$ seconds. The average current is therefore $$I = \frac{qv}{d}$$.

nodes.label: Drift Velocity
nodes.note: Electrons zig-zag between collisions and are nudged only slightly by the field, giving a slow net drift. Its size is $$v_d = \frac{eE\tau}{m} = \frac{eV\tau}{mL}$$, typically under a millimetre per second.

nodes.label: Current Density and Mobility
nodes.note: Current density counts amperes per area and links directly to drift: $$I = neAv_d$$. Mobility is drift per field, $$\mu = \frac{v_d}{E} = \frac{e\tau}{m}$$.

nodes.label: Conductivity and Resistivity
nodes.note: Microscopic Ohm's law reads $$\vec{J} = \sigma\vec{E}$$ with conductivity set by carrier density and collision time: $$\sigma = \frac{ne^2\tau}{m}$$. Resistivity is its reciprocal, $$\rho = \frac{1}{\sigma}$$.

nodes.label: Resistance and Resistivity
nodes.note: Resistance scales with length and shrinks with area, while resistivity belongs to the material alone. The master relation is $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$.

nodes.label: Ohm's Law and Resistance
nodes.note: For ohmic materials voltage and current stay proportional at fixed temperature: $$V = IR$$. Geometry then gives $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$, so shape and material separate cleanly.

nodes.label: Temperature Dependence of Resistance
nodes.note: Metal resistance rises with temperature as lattice vibrations scatter electrons more often: $$R(T) = R_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$$. Semiconductors have negative $$\alpha$$ because thermal carriers multiply.

nodes.label: Stretching and Reducing Wires
nodes.note: Stretching a wire keeps its volume, so gaining length means losing area. If length becomes $$n$$ times, then area becomes $$1/n$$ and $$R' = n^2 R$$; a wire of half the radius has four times the resistance.

nodes.label: Geometry Versus Material
nodes.note: Resistivity depends only on material and temperature, so it survives any reshaping: $$\rho = \frac{m}{ne^2\tau}$$. Charging the temperature changes $$\rho$$, but cutting the wire never does.

nodes.label: Resistor Networks
nodes.note: Complex circuits collapse once series, parallel, and symmetry are recognised. Series adds resistances while parallel adds reciprocals: $$R_{eq} = \sum R_i$$.

nodes.label: Series and Parallel Combinations
nodes.note: Series resistors share current so voltages add, while parallel resistors share voltage so conductances add. $$R_{eq} = \sum_i R_i$$ in series and $$\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \sum_i \frac{1}{R_i}$$ in parallel.

nodes.label: Current and Voltage Division
nodes.note: In a parallel pair current takes the inverse-resistance path, so the bigger resistor gets less: $$I_1 = I\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$. In series the voltage splits in proportion, $$V_1 = V\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}$$.

nodes.label: Delta to Star Transformation
nodes.note: A triangle of resistors can be replaced by a three-legged star whose arms reproduce terminal behaviour. The arms are $$R_1 = \frac{R_bR_c}{R_a + R_b + R_c}$$ and its two cyclic partners.

nodes.label: Cube of Resistors
nodes.note: Symmetry lets the cube's twelve identical edges be folded into three groups of parallel branches. Across an edge the equivalent resistance is $$R_{eq} = \frac{7}{12}R$$, and across a face diagonal it is $$\frac{3}{4}R$$.

nodes.label: Symmetry and Equipotential Removal
nodes.note: Mirror symmetry can force two nodes to the same potential, so no current flows along a bridge between them. Such a branch is deleted, $$I = 0$$, and the circuit factorises.

nodes.label: Kirchhoff's Laws
nodes.note: These two laws encode charge and energy conservation for any multi-loop circuit. Together they give $$\sum I = 0$$ at a junction and $$\sum IR = \sum \mathcal{E}$$ around a loop.

nodes.label: Kirchhoff's Current Law
nodes.note: Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so whatever enters leaves: $$\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}$$. It applies to any element, not just ideal wires.

nodes.label: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law
nodes.note: Going once around a closed loop returns to the same potential, so the total voltage change vanishes: $$\sum \Delta V = 0$$. In practice drops $$IR$$ balance the emfs, giving $$\sum IR = \sum \mathcal{E}$$.

nodes.label: Sign Conventions for Loops
nodes.note: Guess a current direction first and keep it fixed; a negative answer then simply reverses the guess. Traversing a resistor against the assumed current adds $$IR$$, while crossing a cell from minus to plus adds $$\mathcal{E}$$.

nodes.label: Wheatstone and Metre Bridges
nodes.note: Bridges detect the null state, where a galvanometer reads zero and the arms balance exactly. The balance condition is $$\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$$.

nodes.label: Balanced Wheatstone Bridge
nodes.note: When the galvanometer current vanishes, the mid-points are at equal potential and the arms are proportional: $$\frac{P}{Q} = \frac{R}{S}$$. Unbalanced bridges need full Kirchhoff analysis or symmetry tricks.

nodes.label: Metre Bridge
nodes.note: A one-metre wire of uniform resistance acts as two proportional arms with a sliding contact. Balance at $$l$$ cm gives $$\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l}{100 - l}$$, which is why readings cluster near 50 cm.

nodes.label: Why Null Methods Are Preferred
nodes.note: At balance no current flows through the detector, so neither the source nor the meter affects the reading. Accuracy then depends only on length ratios, $$\frac{R}{S} = \frac{l}{100 - l}$$, not on meter calibration.

nodes.label: Cells and Grouping
nodes.note: A real cell has emf $$\mathcal{E}$$ plus internal resistance $$r$$, so terminal voltage shifts with current. Discharging gives $$V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$$.

nodes.label: Terminal Potential Difference
nodes.note: Delivering current makes the terminal voltage sag by the internal drop: $$V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$$. Charging reverses it to $$V = \mathcal{E} + Ir$$, and open circuit leaves $$V = \mathcal{E}$$.

nodes.label: Short Circuit and Load Matching
nodes.note: Shorting a cell drives current limited only by its own resistance: $$I_{sc} = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{r}$$. With a load $$R$$ the delivered current is $$I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R + r}$$.

nodes.label: Series and Parallel Grouping
nodes.note: Series cells add emf and resistance, giving $$I = \frac{n\mathcal{E}}{R + nr}$$ for $$n$$ identical cells. Parallel cells keep emf but divide internal resistance, giving $$I = \frac{m\mathcal{E}}{mR + r}$$, and a reversed cell reduces the net emf.

nodes.label: Mixed Grouping and Maximum Current
nodes.note: With $$n$$ cells in series per row and $$m$$ rows in parallel the current is $$I = \frac{mn\mathcal{E}}{mR + nr}$$. Maximising it requires the external load to equal the bank's internal resistance, $$R = \frac{nr}{m}$$.

nodes.label: Heating, Power and Fuses
nodes.note: Resistive dissipation converts electrical energy to heat, which is both a loss and a design tool. The standard measure is $$H = I^2Rt$$.

nodes.label: Joule's Law of Heating
nodes.note: Heat generated depends on current squared, resistance, and time: $$H = I^2Rt = \frac{V^2}{R}t$$. This is why thin, high-resistance elements run hot.

nodes.label: Electric Power
nodes.note: Power is energy delivered per second in any of the equivalent forms: $$P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$$. Rating an appliance fixes which form is convenient.

nodes.label: Maximum Power Transfer
nodes.note: Power to the load peaks when load resistance equals source internal resistance: $$R = r$$. The peak is $$P_{max} = \frac{\mathcal{E}^2}{4r}$$, delivered at only $$50\%$$ efficiency.

nodes.label: Fuse Wire
nodes.note: A fuse melts when generation outruns cooling along its surface, so only radius matters for rating. That gives $$I^2 \propto r^3$$, hence $$I_{rated} \propto r^{3/2}$$ independent of length.

nodes.label: Potentiometer
nodes.note: A potentiometer compares potentials by balancing them against a uniform wire drop, drawing no current at balance. Its sensitivity is set by the potential gradient $$k = \frac{V}{L}$$.

nodes.label: Principle and Potential Gradient
nodes.note: The wire potential falls linearly with length, so position maps directly to voltage: $$k = \frac{V_{AB}}{L}$$ in volts per metre. A smaller $$k$$ means finer resolution.

nodes.label: Comparison of EMFs
nodes.note: At balance the cell emf equals the wire drop over its balance length, with zero current drawn from the cell. Two cells therefore compare as $$\frac{\mathcal{E}_1}{\mathcal{E}_2} = \frac{l_1}{l_2}$$.

nodes.label: Measurement of Internal Resistance
nodes.note: Balance length falls from $$l_1$$ to $$l_2$$ when a shunt $$R$$ across the cell draws current. The internal resistance follows as $$r = R\left(\frac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right)$$.

nodes.label: RC Transients
nodes.note: A capacitor charges and discharges exponentially, with the resistor setting the clock. The governing time constant is $$\tau = RC$$.

nodes.label: Charging a Capacitor
nodes.note: Charge builds toward its ceiling while current decays from the initial surge: $$q(t) = Q_0\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)$$ and $$i(t) = I_0 e^{-t/RC}$$. One time constant reaches $$63.2\%$$ of full charge.

nodes.label: Discharging and Half Life
nodes.note: With no source the stored charge drains exponentially: $$q(t) = Q_0 e^{-t/RC}$$. Charge halves every $$t_{1/2} = RC\ln 2 \approx 0.693RC$$.

nodes.label: Time Constant and Energy Balance
nodes.note: The time constant sets the response speed, $$\tau = RC$$, after which the circuit is effectively steady. Charging always wastes half the battery's work as heat, $$H = \frac{1}{2}C\mathcal{E}^2$$, whatever $$R$$ is.
